title: IE evidence for sub-shells (period 3 dips); Giant covalent structures
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AS06#t2 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS06#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS06#N.4, BD05#N.7, AS06#N.6, BD05#N.11a, AS06#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sub-shell
items.clue: A division of a main level, such as 3s or 3p, with its own energy.

items.label: Fullerenes
items.clue: Closed cages of C atoms, such as C₆₀, that exist as separate molecules.

items.label: Graphene
items.clue: A single sheet one atom thick that conducts and is very strong for its mass.

items.label: First ionisation energy
items.clue: Needed to remove 1 mol of electrons from 1 mol of gaseous atoms: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.

questions.stem: After the dip, the rise resumes: silicon's first ionisation energy is 787 kJ mol⁻¹, higher than aluminium's 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Why?

options.text: Silicon's electron is removed from 3s, which is lower in energy than aluminium's 3p.
Silicon's two 3p electrons are paired in one orbital, which holds them more firmly.
Silicon atoms are larger, so there is more space for the nucleus to attract its electrons.
Both electrons come from 3p, but silicon has one more proton and similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Same sub-shell, similar shielding, greater nuclear charge: the attraction is stronger, so more energy is needed.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of phosphorus and sulfur are 1012 kJ mol⁻¹ and 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for sulfur is correct?

options.text: Sulfur's outer electrons are shielded by more inner electrons than phosphorus's.
Sulfur's electron is removed from a sub-shell of higher energy than phosphorus's.
Sulfur loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
Sulfur atoms are larger than phosphorus atoms, so their outer electron is further away.

questions.explanation: P has three unpaired 3p electrons; in S one 3p orbital holds a pair. Repulsion between them means slightly less energy is needed.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity far better along its layers than at right angles to them. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other, and charge is carried only in the direction they slide.
Its ions lie between the layers, so they can move only in the plane of the layers.
Each atom forms four bonds within its layer, so no electrons are left to pass between layers.
Its delocalised electrons move freely within a layer, but cannot easily cross the gap to the next.

questions.explanation: Each C bonds to three others; its fourth electron is delocalised over its own layer only. So charge flows easily along a layer, but hardly between layers.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of beryllium and boron are 900 kJ mol⁻¹ and 801 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for boron is correct?

options.text: Boron's electron is removed from a 2p orbital that already holds another electron.
Boron atoms are larger than beryllium atoms, so the outer electron is further away.
Boron's electron is removed from 2p, which is higher in energy than beryllium's 2s.
Boron's nuclear charge is shared among more electrons, so each is held less strongly.
